title: Spec changes
summary: What differs between the specs of two branches, by item and requirement.
description:
A line diff of the JSON files says which lines changed. This says what changed in the spec: which items and requirements were added, removed or reworded.

It compares a base (by default the default branch) with another branch or commit.

stories.as: someone deciding whether a branch is ready
stories.want: to see what its spec promises that the main branch's doesn't, and what it takes away
stories.soThat: I judge the change by what it means

requirements.text: Items are matched by id. An item only one side has is added or removed; one that differs is changed; one that is the same isn't listed. A file with the same git object id on both sides is the same without being read, so only what differs is read.

history.text: Items are matched by id. An item only one side has is added or removed; one that differs is changed; one that is the same isn't listed.
history.reason: Comparing had to work for specs too large to read whole.

requirements.text: Requirements are matched by id. A reworded requirement shows its old and new text with the words that differ marked.

history.text: Requirements are matched by their id within the item. A reworded requirement shows its old and new text with the words that differ marked.
history.reason: Requirement ids became unique in the whole spec, so an id means the same requirement wherever it is.

requirements.text: A requirement whose level or status changed shows the old and the new value. Leaving `level` out and writing `must` are the same.
Changes are listed in the outline's order, with removed items and requirements where they used to be.
A figure whose file changed shows the picture from both sides. A changed caption alone doesn't.
A summary counts the added, changed, moved and removed items and requirements.

history.text: A summary counts the added, changed and removed items and requirements.
history.reason: Moved items and requirements are told apart from added and removed ones, and counted as such.

requirements.text: A pull request that touches `.spec` shows these changes in its Files tab, and links to them on their own.

history.text: A pull request that touches `.spec` links to the changes between its base branch and its head commit.
history.reason: A link to another screen wasn't a review: the changes had to be where the files are reviewed.

requirements.text: A side without a spec counts as an empty one: everything on the other side is added or removed.
In the comparison of two branches, each changed item opens in the spec browser, on the side that has it.

history.text: Each changed item opens in the spec browser, on the side that has it.
history.reason: Inside a pull request the card is a file under review and carries the file's menu instead.

requirements.text: An item whose file moved is shown once, as moved, with whatever else changed in it. A move is known from a pull request's renames, or from the file's contents being unchanged.

Changes that take something away from the spec are pointed out, in a list above the changes and on each item and requirement: a deleted requirement or item (it should have been deprecated), a deprecation with its reason, a lowered level, a status that went back.

history.text: Changes that make the spec promise less are pointed out, in a list above the changes and on each item and requirement: a removed must or should requirement, a lowered level, a status that went back, a removed item with live requirements.
history.reason: Nothing is deleted from a spec any more: what is no longer wanted is deprecated. So every deletion is pointed out, not only those of must and should requirements.

requirements.text: The requirements a change left alone can be unfolded for context.
The changes can be narrowed to added, changed, moved, removed, or those that take something away. They are shown `spec-diff.page` at a time, and each is drawn when it nears the screen.
A requirement that moved to another item is shown as moved, at both ends, with what changed on the way. It doesn't count as removed, and isn't flagged as a promise taken away.

A requirement with a new version shows the version it went from and to, with the reason its history gives. One whose text or level changed at the same version is marked: right for a wording fix, for the reviewer to judge.
A history that was rewritten, shortened, or that doesn't record the version just left as it was, is flagged with what takes something away. So is a version that went back.
